title: Leadership Is Complex, Not Complicated
author: Luca Foppoli
summary: Responding to a piece by fellow Substack writer Leon Flux, Foppoli argues that leadership resists solution precisely because it is a complex adaptive system problem rather than a complicated one, using the contrast between a catapult launching a projectile (predictable, complicated) and a catapult launching a live pigeon (unpredictable, complex) to illustrate the difference. He traces how twentieth-century management theory, particularly Taylorism, tried to force leadership into the complicated category by stripping judgment out of work and treating people as replaceable, standardized parts -- an approach he says worked on factory floors but produces disengagement in knowledge work. Foppoli argues this same complicated-solution instinct persists today in mandated return-to-office policies, which attempt to manufacture collaboration by scheduling it rather than building the conditions for it. His practical prescription for managers is to treat teams as complex adaptive systems that can only be 'nudged,' through coaching individuals and architecting team structure and communication flows, rather than solved through a single correct intervention. He closes by reframing the manager's job: not to find the solution, but to build structure, coach people, and let results emerge from a system that is, by nature, still evolving.
points: Foppoli's central distinction: complicated systems (like a catapult launching a projectile) have a knowable 'right' answer; complex adaptive systems (like a catapult launching a live pigeon) do not, because they learn and adapt.

He argues Taylorism succeeded on the factory floor by stripping judgment from work, but failed in knowledge work because removing judgment from a system that runs on judgment produced disengagement and output below expectations.
Mandated return-to-office policies are framed as a modern instance of the same complicated-solution fallacy: an attempt to summon collaboration by scheduling it.

His two-part prescription for managers: 'nudging the parts' (coaching individuals through positive reinforcement) and 'building the structure' (designing team governance and communication flow) -- both described as never-ending, not one-time fixes.
Closing reframe: 'In leadership, stop looking for the solution. Build the structure, coach the people and let the results emerge.'
quotes: In a complicated system the total is the sum of the parts and knowing each part gives you a full understanding of the whole system, its behavior and output. Complicated problems have a "right" solution.
In a complex systems the total is more than the sum of its parts and knowing the single pieces is not enough to reliably predict how the system will behave.

Taylorism addressed the problem by removing its complex aspects: it transformed people into cogs of the factory process, forcing them to adhere to strict instructions, measuring their output with scientific precision and treating them as replaceable parts.
This approach failed miserably when applied to knowledge work, as removing judgment from a system that runs on judgment produced disengagement, output below expectations and a machine that grinds.

See the recent wave of mandated return to office (an attempt to summon collaboration by scheduling it, which will only obtain bodies at desks on Tuesdays) and the number of prescriptive dickheads still successfully climbing the corporate ladder.
People are complex. Embrace it. Own it. Treat them as such and you will be amazed at what they will achieve.
